guides.title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
guides.short_title: Basket or oven? Start with your dinner.
guides.dek: One basket, two baskets, or French doors. Make the format decision before you get lost in presets.
guides.takeaway: Choose a format around the food you cook and the space you have—not the biggest number on the box.

sections.heading: First, picture an ordinary dinner.
paragraphs: Write down the meal you make on a busy evening. Are you cooking one thing, or trying to finish two different foods together? Do you want a drawer you can pull out, or an oven-style door? These are shopping questions, not a verdict on which appliance cooks better.

The three listings below offer a useful starting point: one title names two independent baskets, another names a French-door oven, and the third names a basket. Their names describe different layouts; they do not establish cooking performance.

sections.heading: Do not let “oven” make the decision for you.
paragraphs: The Chefman 6-quart listing calls itself an “Air Fryer Oven” and also names “2 Independent 3Qt” baskets. Read the whole description of the format rather than comparing one headline word.
Put the total capacity and the capacity of each cooking compartment in separate notes. A two-basket layout is not the same buying question as a single uninterrupted cooking space.

sections.heading: Make the comparison on your own counter.
checklist: Measure your available width, depth and height.
Check the exact model’s manual for operating clearance and ventilation; those measurements are not verified here.
Allow room to open the door or pull out the drawer.
Compare the parts you will handle and wash after a normal meal.
Only then check the current price and included accessories on Amazon.

unknowns: Usable basket/interior dimensions and operating clearance.
Cooking speed, evenness, noise and energy use.
Which format is best for your kitchen.

guides.title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
guides.short_title: What does that capacity number actually tell you?
guides.dek: A larger number is not a meal plan. Here is what to check before you compare quarts.
guides.takeaway: Compare the space the food will use, not just the capacity printed in the title.

sections.heading: Separate the total from the compartments.
paragraphs: The Chefman dual-basket title gives both “6 Quart” and “2 Independent 3Qt” baskets. Keep those numbers separate. The 8 Qt Chefman title names a basket; the Emeril Lagasse title says “26QT” and “Extra Large Interior”.
Those are listing descriptions—not a measured comparison of usable cooking area. We have not converted any of them into servings, portions or family size.

sections.heading: Take a meal-shaped note.
paragraphs: Before opening another tab, note the food you need to fit and whether you expect to cook it in one layer. Then look for the internal dimensions or a model-specific manual. If you cannot find them, ask the manufacturer rather than guessing from the capacity label.
checklist: Is the number total capacity or per compartment?
Are you comparing the same unit?
What are the usable internal dimensions?
Will the food fit the way the manual instructs?
Where will you store the parts when not in use?

sections.heading: Know when not to make the upgrade.
paragraphs: If the larger model does not solve a specific space or cooking-layout problem, leave the decision open. A capacity label alone is not evidence of better results. Return to the basket-versus-oven guide to compare the format first.

unknowns: Usable cooking area, internal dimensions and portion counts.
How much food can be cooked evenly in each model.

guides.title: How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs
guides.short_title: The part after dinner deserves a look, too.
guides.dek: Think beyond the footprint. Check the opening space, removable parts and model-specific care instructions.
guides.takeaway: Measure the working space, then check how you will clean every food-contact part.

sections.heading: An appliance needs working space, not just a parking space.
paragraphs: Mark out the place you would put it. Check whether a drawer can pull out fully or a door can open without meeting another appliance. Read the model-specific manual for ventilation and operating clearances. We have not verified those measurements for these products.
None of the three listing titles gives width, depth or height. Do not turn a photograph or capacity number into a dimension.

sections.heading: Read the cleaning wording one part at a time.
paragraphs: The two Chefman titles use dishwasher-safe wording for their baskets. That wording does not tell you how to clean every other component. The Emeril title names six cooking accessories but does not establish their care requirements.
Use the current manual to check each removable part, its coating and any dishwasher restrictions. We have not tested cleanup effort or coating durability.

sections.heading: A five-minute shopping check.
checklist: Measure available counter width, depth and overhead space.
Find the exact model’s clearance instructions.
Check where the hot parts can safely rest.
List each food-contact part and its care instructions.
Make sure the parts fit your sink, dishwasher or storage space.

unknowns: External dimensions, ventilation clearances and cord lengths.
Care requirements for all accessories; coating durability.
Hands-on cleaning time.

guides.title: Questions before buying a multi-function kitchen appliance
guides.short_title: More presets. But more useful to you?
guides.dek: Before you count the functions, make a list of the ones you would actually use.
guides.takeaway: Match the functions to real meals and verify the included parts. A preset count is not a performance score.

sections.heading: Start with the tasks you already do.
paragraphs: Make a short list: what do you cook, what do you reheat, and which existing appliance would this replace? Keep the functions you would use and set the rest aside. This is an editorial exercise, not a claim that any model replaces another.
The Emeril title says “24 One-Touch Preset Options”. The Chefman 8 Qt title says “4-in-1” and names Bake, Dehydrate and Frozen. We have not verified the full preset menus or compared the results.

sections.heading: Check what you need to use each function.
checklist: What does the setting actually do, according to the manual?
Does it require an accessory, and is that accessory included?
Does using one function prevent another from running at the same time?
Will you need to rearrange shelves or baskets?
How will you clean and store the extra parts?

sections.heading: Leave unsupported claims out of the decision.
paragraphs: We have not measured cooking speed, running cost or results. We do not use preset totals to name a winner. If those are your deciding factors, seek model-specific testing with a described method before choosing.

unknowns: Complete preset definitions, accessory contents and simultaneous-function limitations.
Results, speed and energy consumption under comparable conditions.

guides.title: Instant-read or wireless thermometer: which questions matter?
guides.short_title: Spot check or connected probe? Ask this first.
guides.dek: Two thermometer formats, different shopping questions. Start with how you want to take a reading.
guides.type: A different kind of kitchen tool
guides.takeaway: Choose the reading workflow, then check the manual. Do not treat a product’s advertised speed or accuracy as an independent test.

sections.heading: Separate a reading from a monitoring setup.
paragraphs: The ThermoMaven listing names a digital meat thermometer. The CHEF iQ listing names a smart wireless meat thermometer with three probes. Those are the two formats on this shortlist—not proof that either will suit every grill, oven or air fryer.

Ask whether you want to check food at a moment in time or use a connected probe setup. Then confirm the exact model’s permitted use, probe placement and heat limits in its manual. Do not leave a handheld probe in an appliance unless its instructions explicitly allow it.

sections.heading: Treat connection claims as questions to answer.
checklist: Does the setup require an app, account, Wi-Fi or another device?
Which parts are allowed inside the appliance, and at what temperatures?
How should each probe be placed, cleaned and stored?
What happens if the connection or battery is lost?
What calibration or accuracy information does the manufacturer provide for this exact model?

sections.heading: Use food-safety guidance for the target temperature.
paragraphs: FoodSafety.gov says to use a food thermometer to check that food has reached a safe minimum internal temperature, and notes that some foods also need rest time. Use its food-specific chart rather than a product advertisement to choose the target.

We have not tested either thermometer’s accuracy, response time, wireless range or food-safety alerts. A certification claim in a listing title is not independent certification verification by this publication.

unknowns: Independent accuracy and response-time measurements.
App compatibility, connection behaviour, battery life and exact operating limits.
Certification records for the advertised exact models.

guides.title: Hosting dinner? Make a kitchen shortlist before you buy.
guides.short_title: Hosting season, without the impulse buy.
guides.dek: A meal-first checklist for the counter space, cooking format and temperature tools you might need.
guides.takeaway: Plan the meal first. Buy a tool only when it solves a named problem in that plan.

sections.heading: Write the menu before the shopping list.
paragraphs: List what needs cooking, when you want to serve it and which equipment you already have. Circle the actual bottleneck: space, a cooking compartment, an awkward tray, or taking a temperature reading. A new appliance is one option, not the default answer.
This is a seasonal planning exercise, not a claim about deals, availability, search demand or products selling out. We publish no sale prices or countdowns.

sections.heading: Give each possible purchase one job.
checklist: For an air fryer: which meal and which cooking layout are you buying it for?
For an oven-style appliance: have you checked operating clearance and door space?
For a thermometer: how will you take the reading, and have you read the correct-use instructions?
For accessories: are the exact parts included or a separate purchase?
For any new tool: where will you clean and store it after dinner?

sections.heading: Keep safe cooking separate from marketing.
paragraphs: Use the official FoodSafety.gov temperature chart for the food you are serving, including any rest time. A preset name, an appliance mode or a thermometer feature is not a substitute for food-specific guidance.
If your existing equipment covers the plan, your shortlist can stay empty. The useful outcome is a decision—not necessarily a purchase.

unknowns: Your menu, available counter space and existing equipment.
Any retailer promotion or delivery promise; none is asserted here.

guides.title: What do “Hi-Fry”, “Sync Finish” and “4-in-1” actually promise?
guides.short_title: What the words on an air-fryer listing promise.
guides.dek: Three marketing names from three listings, read closely — what each one says, and the question it leaves you to answer yourself.
guides.takeaway: These are names inside product titles, not standards with a definition we can read from the listing. Quote the words, expect the manual to carry the meaning, and treat any performance promise as the brand’s claim rather than ours.

sections.heading: Start with what each title actually says.
paragraphs: The CHEFMAN dual-basket listing names “Sync Finish, Hi-Fry, Auto Shutoff” among its features. The Chefman TurboFry listing names a “4-in-1” with a “450°F Hi-Fry Option for Crispier Results”. The Emeril Lagasse listing names “Multi-Function”, “24 One-Touch Preset Options”, “Extra Large Interior” and “Six Cooking Accessories Included”. Those are the words on the page; a page title is not a specification sheet.

Notice that the same word travels. “Hi-Fry” appears as a bare feature in one listing and as a named temperature option in another. Before you decide what it is worth, ask the question that only the exact model can answer: what does the control actually change — temperature, time, fan speed, or a preset that does all three?
checklist: Which of these words appear in the title, and which appear only in a spec table?
Does the feature have a number attached, or is it a name with no stated behaviour?
Do two listings in the same shortlist use one word for two different things?
Is the accessory or setting required for that feature present in the box?

sections.heading: A preset count and a function count are not the same number.
paragraphs: “24 One-Touch Preset Options” and “4-in-1” are counting different things. One counts programmes; the other counts advertised cooking modes, and the TurboFry title names three of them in words you can read: bake, dehydrate, frozen. Neither number tells you how a preset behaves, whether it can be adjusted, or what happens when you override it.

So the useful comparison is not which listing has the bigger number. It is whether you can see, for the exact model, what each mode sets, whether a mode needs an accessory that is in the box, and where the instructions live when you want the definition rather than the label.

sections.heading: What a listing word cannot do.
paragraphs: It cannot become a claim by us. Amazon’s Program Policies prohibit inaccurate, overbroad, deceptive or otherwise misleading statements about a product, and the FTC is blunt about experience: you cannot talk about a product you have not tried. That is why this guide quotes titles and stops there. “Nonstick dishwasher-safe baskets” is the brand’s wording about its own listing; whether your dishwasher, your rack position and your usage match that wording is a manual-and-common-sense check, not something we can confirm from a title.
We have not tested any of these three appliances, and we are not verifying the brand’s claims by repeating them. Where the label is the only source, the label is what we show.

unknowns: What “Sync Finish”, “Hi-Fry”, “Auto Shutoff” or any preset does mechanically on a specific model.
Whether the named temperature option changes peak temperature, cook time, or both.
Whether a claimed accessory, mode or feature is required for the result described in the title.
Any performance outcome: crisping, evenness, noise, cleanup effort or durability. Nothing here was tested.

guides.title: How do you know when an air-fryer cook is actually done?
guides.short_title: Is it done? Check the food, not the timer.
guides.dek: A beep says time passed. A temperature says the food reached a target. Here is how to separate the two without owning a lab.
guides.takeaway: Use the appliance for heat and a thermometer for the decision. FoodSafety.gov publishes minimum internal temperatures by food; check against those, and treat any doneness cue from the appliance as a starting point rather than a verdict.

sections.heading: Separate “cooking finished” from “safe to eat”.
paragraphs: FoodSafety.gov’s chart is blunt: use a food thermometer to check that food has reached a safe minimum internal temperature, and note that some meats also need rest time so the innermost parts finish cooking. Its figures for the foods a kitchen air fryer is usually asked for: chicken, turkey and other poultry 165°F (74°C); ground meat and sausage 160°F (71°C); beef, bison, veal, goat and lamb steaks, roasts and chops 145°F (63°C) with a three-minute rest; casseroles and leftovers 165°F (74°C).

That chart is a food-safety reference, not a recipe, and we are reproducing it rather than restyling it: it was last reviewed 21 Nov 2024 by the source, and it is the kind of page worth reading before you decide what to look for.

sections.heading: What the listing can tell you about signals — and what it cannot.
paragraphs: The CHEFMAN dual-basket title names “Auto Shutoff”. A shut-off behaviour is a safety and convenience feature; it is not a doneness test, and the title does not say what triggers it. The Chefman TurboFry title names a “450°F Hi-Fry Option for Crispier Results”, which is a claim about a result, not a measurement you can read off the food.

So the appliance can end the cycle. It is the food that answers the question. If a timer, a beep and a thermometer disagree, trust the thermometer — and then write down what you found, because that note is worth more next season than a remembered impression.

sections.heading: A checking routine that survives a real dinner.
checklist: Check the thickest part, away from bone and away from the pan surface.
Let the reading settle before you record it — and record it, with the food and the setting you used.
Clean the probe between raw and ready-to-eat food.
Confirm the maximum temperature your thermometer allows in an appliance before you leave it in one; check the exact model’s instructions rather than a listing title.
If the target is not reached, keep cooking and check again. Rest time counts for some meats, so measure after it, not instead of it.
Reheat leftovers to the figure the chart gives for leftovers, not to “warm through”.

unknowns: How accurate or fast either listed thermometer is; none of that was tested here.
Whether a specific air-fryer model signals completion in a way that matches its timer.
Cooking times for any food in any of these appliances. No timing table is claimed from a listing.
Whether an appliance’s stated temperature equals the food’s temperature at the probe.

questions.question: Who reads a guide before it ships, and against what?
questions.known: Every guide is published under the “Zone3 Editorial” byline, states that it is not a hands-on review, and each section carries official source links. No approval record exists in the repository.
questions.missing: A named approver, the checklist they apply (disclosure placement, sponsored rels, source dates, absent values, no experience claims) and where an approval is recorded.
questions.default: Publish only listing-linked copy under the organisation byline, and keep “not a hands-on review” on every guide.
questions.discovery: Write a five-line pre-publication checklist, name who signs it, and store the sign-off date with the guide record in the register — not in a private note.
questions.blocks: Any increase in publishing cadence; any claim stronger than a listing quote
questions.answer_form: A checklist file in the repository and an approver name (or an explicit “no human review yet”, which caps what the copy may claim).

questions.question: Is anyone going to cook in these appliances, and at what cost?
questions.known: Decision S-06 (“what the appliance is like to live with”) is recorded as not adopted because no testing evidence exists. Google’s review guidance asks for original evidence and support for any “best” recommendation; the FTC states you cannot talk about your experience with a product you have not tried.
questions.missing: Whether units will be bought or borrowed, who tests, what is measured, how failures are recorded, and who owns the photographs.
questions.default: Keep publishing questions and listing wording. Add no tested verdict, no “we liked”, no winner.
questions.discovery: Before ordering anything, write the protocol: models, tasks, repetitions, what counts as a measurement, how a failure is reported, and the disclosure that this is a home kitchen, not a lab.
questions.blocks: Tested comparisons, product photography, any ranking or “best of” page, decision S-06
questions.answer_form: Either a protocol plus unit access and dated result rows, or a written “no testing” that keeps the editorial ceiling where it is.

questions.question: What happens to a guide after it is published — and what would make us change it?
questions.known: The recorded cadence is one guide reviewed every 14 days, publication gated on evidence. The feed and sitemap are register-driven, so a new guide reaches both automatically. Production analytics is off, so no page has measured performance.
questions.missing: The trigger rules: what evidence would cause a rewrite, a merge, or a retirement, and who notices.
questions.default: Re-verify the sources of an existing guide before writing another one; never refresh a page by changing its date alone.
questions.discovery: Define three dated triggers: source page moved or removed, a Search Console report showing a query the guide does not answer, or a product listing withdrawn. Each one maps to a specific action in the register.
questions.blocks: A defensible refresh policy; retirement of pages whose sources went stale
questions.answer_form: Three trigger rules written into the cadence note, each with the action it forces and where the evidence is stored.

questions.question: Is the Associates account actually enrolled, and does this site belong to it?
questions.known: The brief supplied the tracking ID “shopnow047c-20”. The repository has no account access, so assignment, standing and reports are unverified. Each of the five submitted links opened a product listing, which shows a destination, not an attribution.
questions.missing: Enrolment status, whether the ID belongs to the account, whether the site is registered in it, and the Amazon account-side view of the submitted short links.
questions.default: Leave FLG-003 unresolved. Do not call the supplied links invalid; do not call them validated. Keep intended identifiers separate from observed redirects.
questions.discovery: In the Associates account: confirm the site is listed, the tracking ID matches, and create one Special Link per product. Compare its destination with the observed one. Record the date and the outcome in the intent register — never paste account screenshots into the repository, they carry identifiers.
questions.blocks: Every revenue-adjacent statement; replacing submitted links; scaling to more products
questions.answer_form: A dated line per product: enrolled workflow, link created, destination matches intent, tracking ID shown in the URL parameter.

questions.question: Is the site two categories or one?
questions.known: Five submitted links, two categories: three air fryers and two meat thermometers, with six published guides split across them plus one seasonal piece. Amazon’s own breadcrumb on the air-fryer listing runs Home & Kitchen › Kitchen & Dining › Small Appliances › Fryers › Air Fryers.
questions.missing: Whether the thermometer listings stay in scope, and whether the site is a kitchen-tools publication or an air-fryer publication with a side table.
questions.default: Keep both categories under one kitchen brand and add no third category while traffic is unmeasured.
questions.discovery: Decide the scope before adding topics: a second category needs its own cluster of guides and its own pillar page, not one article sharing a front door with unrelated copy.
questions.blocks: Topic calendar, category pages, internal-link structure
questions.answer_form: One sentence of scope, plus a yes/no on the two thermometer listings staying in the shortlist.

questions.question: What evidence will define 'organic traffic success', and when is it reviewed?
questions.known: Search Console is not verified and no query data exists; the 14-day cadence is an operating plan, not a traffic result.

questions.discovery: Verify the property and submit the sitemap, then write the success definition into the decision record and review it only on the stated date with new dated reports.

Whether any manufacturer would supply a review unit.

Whether API access will be requested and under which program.

Which provider and consent wording would be acceptable.

proposals.next: Shape the existing evidence practice into one public 'how we put a guide together' method page built only from what the repo already does (dated captures, source links, intent record, flagged register). Publish nothing new as fact; describe the method itself.

Whether a described method step matches what the build chain actually does

Which evidence links each chosen path carries

What license or permission conditions attach to the chosen path

Whether the listings change on the re-observation date

Whether a chooser above the comparison table changes which guides readers open (measured later, once collection is authorized)

Whether a sticky format bar names the column in view correctly

discoveries: Which first-party metric the owner accepts as the success definition
What the first dated report shows for that metric and window

Whether a draft post passes the disclosure checklist and the FTC guidance test

design_prompt.intro: Ten blocks, each doing one job. Paste the whole brief into a design tool or hand a designer one block at a time. Every block is grounded either in a rule already recorded in this repository or in an official policy page, and none of them asks you to assert a fact the site does not have.

blocks.heading: 1 · The job of every page
blocks.text: A reader arrives with a question about a thing on their counter. The page answers four things in this order: what the linked listing actually says, what it does not say, what the reader should check at home, and where the sponsored link goes. Anything unverified is left visibly absent, with the gap named. A page that cannot answer all four is a note, not a guide.

blocks.heading: 2 · Voice, and the words this site does not use
blocks.text: Second person, plain verbs, short sentences, one idea each. No “must-have”, “game-changer”, “obsessed”, “top-rated”, “we loved”, “In conclusion”, no countdowns, no invented urgency, no fake expert, no first-person experience of a product nobody used. Every product statement names the listing it came from, and the date it was read. The read-aloud test is the editor: a sentence you would not say at a dinner table gets rewritten.

blocks.heading: 3 · Architecture, top to bottom
blocks.text: Masthead → non-dismissible disclosure strip immediately under it → one editorial promise (not a value proposition) → the shortlist, filterable, cards carrying format illustration and the listing’s own words → a question router → the guide index → one seasonal cluster → a comparison table whose unverified cells are blank and labelled → footer that keeps the whole research set reachable in a single group. Product first, verification process second, always.

blocks.heading: 4 · Visual system
blocks.text: Ivory canvas, deep green ink, one warm accent, hairline rules, generous rhythm. Serif display at 46–79px with tight leading, sans body at 15–17px with 1.8–1.95 line-height. Minimum 44px tap targets, visible focus ring, tables that scroll inside a labelled region. No gradient headline, no glass, no shadow soup, no card grid without a reason. Art is diagrammatic and generic, never a stand-in for a photograph of the SKU.

blocks.heading: 5 · What pictures are allowed here
blocks.text: Two kinds only: a labelled AI editorial still life, and original format diagrams drawn for this site. No Amazon Program Content asset is downloaded or stored; no scraped photography; no image that implies a test result, a meal we cooked, or the exact look of a listed model. If real product photography ever appears, it is ours, dated, and captioned with who shot it.

blocks.heading: 6 · Disclosure, links and the things that must never be improvised
blocks.text: The Associates statement appears under the masthead on every page and again in the footer. Every Amazon link carries rel="sponsored" and names its destination in the CTA copy. The tag-parameter requirement, the no-bookmarking rule and the no-association-of-sub-tags-with-users rule are treated as design constraints, not fine print. Prices and availability appear only where Amazon serves them or an API licence covers them. Any mention of a limited-time promotion inherits the duty to remove it when the promotion ends.

blocks.heading: 7 · The editorial system
blocks.text: One question per page, question-shaped titles, a short-answer box at the top, three body sections that each carry their source links, an explicit “what we have not established” block, and related reads that go somewhere a reader actually needs. Cadence: review one guide every 14 days; publish only through the gate. Keep the ladder honest — published, buildable from the listings already read, and held. A held piece stays held; softening the gate to ship it is how a publication becomes a content farm.

blocks.heading: 8 · Topics that fit this shelf
blocks.text: Write the buyer question the listing leaves open: what “Sync Finish” and “Hi-Fry” actually name, how quart counts mislead, whether two small baskets beat one big one, what a preset does when you press it, how to know a cook is done, what cleanup costs you in counter space, and how a probe changes a roast. Trending framing is allowed only as dated context (“it is hosting season”), never as a popularity claim, and never as a reason to invent a search-volume number.

blocks.heading: 9 · Measurement without a surveillance build
blocks.text: Five first-party events, aggregate by UTC day, no cookies, no identifiers, no fingerprints, honouring Global Privacy Control, Do Not Track and Save-Data, and staying off until a durable host exists. A verified Search Console property and dated first-party reports are the only inputs that pick the next topic. A click is not an order; an order is not a trend.

blocks.heading: 10 · Definition of done
blocks.text: The documented chain runs twice and the second run changes nothing; every gate passes; every current table row carries a dated official source or an honest blank; no page loses its disclosure or its sponsored rel; the deployed page is fetched and read back. Then re-measure the counts — pages, guides, sources, flags — and put both readings in the register. “Polished” has to be a number that moved, not a sentence in a changelog.

blocks.heading: Batch-2 directions (session e61f5735)
blocks.text: Add a which-one-is-for-you chooser above the comparison table and keep the comparison thumb-first on small screens, so a phone reader never silently loses a column. Refresh for real, sourced calendar moments instead of invented seasons, and make the verification method itself visible trust content: dated sources, stated limits, blanks left blank. Route social or video distribution through the same disclosure rule as the site. Keep topics chosen from measured first-party queries once they exist, never from instinct or imagined trends, and record every accepted suggestion as a dated decision with its evidence before anything is implemented.

blocks.heading: 12 · Polished affiliate shopfront (batch 3, session d3493182)
blocks.text: Paste-ready prompt for a design tool or a designer. Build a polished affiliate shopfront that reads like a publication, not a register, using only facts already in the register. Front page, top to bottom: masthead with the disclosure directly underneath; a hero that names the reader's question (not a product claim); the five-product shortlist as cards, each with its original format illustration, the listing's own capacity wording, a two-sided fit note (fits you if / not for you if) and one sponsored call to action; a comparison table whose every cell is either sourced or visibly blank; the guide index as question-shaped cards; one restrained dated seasonal strip that states a calendar fact and links the guides that answer it; a footer directory that keeps every dashboard surface reachable. Category pages repeat the same card system. Guides keep one question per page, the evidence limit stated on the page, and related links to the comparison, a buying guide and the category pillar. Mobile first: readable type scale, 44-pixel tap targets, the comparison reachable without horizontal hunting. Voice: second person, plain verbs, short sentences; never use must-have, game-changer, obsessed, top-rated, we loved, In conclusion, countdowns, invented urgency, a fake expert, or any trending, best, number-one, price, rating or test claim the register does not hold. Images: labelled generic art only until a licensed-photo decision is recorded. Catchy working titles for the next guides (editorial hypotheses, not demand claims): Two baskets or one big one? What to compare before you buy. How many quarts is dinner for two — and for four? What does Hi-Fry actually promise on the label? Where does the probe go? Turkey, ham and roasts, checked the boring way. Counter-space math: measure before you believe the quart number. Is it done? Check the food, not the timer. Hosting season: make a shortlist before you buy. Instant-read or wireless: which questions matter first? Definition of done: the full release chain passes twice with a clean diff, every table row carries a dated official source or a labelled blank, no page loses its disclosure or sponsored links, and the page-experience baseline is re-measured and recorded.

suggestion_intake.title: The shape a new suggestion has to take
suggestion_intake.note: Anyone proposing work for this site — including a build session — writes it in this shape. It is what makes two suggestions comparable, and it is what stops a confident paragraph from becoming a plan.
fields: One sentence a reader would notice, not a component name.
The problem it removes, in evidence terms.
The question IDs from the register below that must be answered first.
A link to the rule or guidance that shapes the option.
What the site does if nobody ever answers.
Open, blocked on owner, blocked on evidence, or needs a budget decision.

review_b9008684.intro: A dated review round, kept separate from the six standing proposals above. Every card is review-only: choosing an option saves a note in this browser and implements nothing. Each suggestion carries the sentence it would add to the design prompt and what evidence would change the decision.

design_feed.title: Ship a dated seasonal strip, not a hype banner
design_feed.why: Late November through December is when the thermometer guides and the hosting checklist are naturally useful, and a calendar fact needs no demand claim. A restrained strip that says what today is and links the three guides that answer it makes the site feel tended rather than generated.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Carry one restrained, dated seasonal strip that connects existing guides to the current cooking season; it states calendar facts only, never demand, popularity or trend claims.
design_feed.falsifier: If the strip dates badly or its guides draw no measurable engagement after the season, retire it — a stale strip is worse than none.

design_feed.title: Approve the article slate below, one guide at a time
design_feed.why: The reading room grows credibility by rhythm, not volume: one new question-shaped guide at a time, each through the same publishing gate, each linked from two existing guides so the cluster stays one hop wide.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Grow the reading room one question-shaped guide at a time; every new guide keeps the same evidence limits, related-links mesh, schema, canonical URL, sitemap and RSS entry as the current six.
design_feed.falsifier: A drafted guide that cannot cite its sources, or that repeats a question the room already answers, does not ship.

design_feed.status: Proposed — needs sourced Q&A pairs first
design_feed.title: Add FAQPage structured data only where every answer is already sourced and visible
design_feed.why: Article schema ships today. An FAQ block earns rich results only when the answers are actually on the page, and Google is explicit that invisible or empty-page markup is out of bounds — so the constraint is the editor, not the schema.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Add a short FAQ block to a guide only when every answer is already stated and sourced in that guide, and mark it up with FAQPage structured data; never mark up content the page does not show.
design_feed.falsifier: If an answer needs a fact the register cannot source, the question is dropped, not inferred.

design_feed.status: Proposed — needs a layout audit first
design_feed.title: Port the mobile pass into the reader template: type scale, tap targets, a sticky way to reach the comparison
design_feed.why: The research layer already ships a clamped type scale, 44-pixel tap targets and a sticky quick-compare bar; the reader template should carry the same discipline so long guides keep the comparison one thumb-reach away.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Keep a mobile-first type scale, 44-pixel minimum tap targets, and a sticky way to reach the format comparison from long guides.
design_feed.falsifier: If the sticky bar overlaps content or traps scrolling on any viewport, simplify it rather than patch it.

design_feed.status: Blocked — needs the owner’s imagery decision (S-18)
design_feed.title: Decide the product-imagery route before any photography ships
design_feed.why: Three routes exist and they need different permissions: keep labelled generic art (no new permissions), authorized Amazon-served or API imagery if API access is ever established, or original photography of owned units provided by the owner. The default stands until someone chooses.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Use labelled generic art until authorized exact-product assets exist; when real imagery arrives, label its source and date next to the listing facts it illustrates.
design_feed.falsifier: Unpublished while blocked; the decision record names the route before any image changes.

design_feed.status: Proposed — needs an internal-linking look first
design_feed.title: Group the reading room by the decision a reader is facing
design_feed.why: The six guides already answer a sequence — format, capacity, cleanup, functions, thermometer, hosting — but the index presents them as one flat grid. A visible grouping makes the hub structure the buyer can feel, not just the links the crawler sees.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Group the reading room by the decision a reader is facing, not by product type alone, so every guide is one visible hop from its two neighbours.
design_feed.falsifier: If readers still arrive on cards without context after grouping, revisit the grouping rather than adding navigation.

design_feed.title: Keep review mode review-only, and give every suggestion a falsifier
design_feed.why: This round’s cards each carry a “what would change our mind” line; future decision surfaces should keep the same select/save/export pattern with no implementation path, so a review can never quietly become a change.
design_feed.feeds_prompt: Every suggestion shows what evidence would change the decision; a review choice never implements itself.
design_feed.falsifier: If any future page lets a review action publish, spend or reconfigure, that page fails review.

article_slate.title: Where does the probe go? Turkey, ham and roasts, checked the boring way.
article_slate.angle: Probe placement, rest times and the safe minimum temperatures as the factual spine; the thermometer listings appear as tools, not verdicts.
article_slate.provenance: The safe-temperature chart on FoodSafety.gov (poultry 165°F; 145°F plus a 3-minute rest for whole cuts), read 2026-11-19.
article_slate.seasonal: Timed to late-November through December cooking; stated as a calendar fact, never as a demand claim.

article_slate.title: Can one air fryer cover a holiday table — or do you need two drawers?
article_slate.angle: Capacity and format questions under one roof: what a quart number can and cannot tell you about fitting a real meal, and when two independent baskets change the plan.
article_slate.provenance: Listing format wording for the three air-fryer destinations, observed 2026-11-19; no performance claim.
article_slate.seasonal: Same calendar window as AS-01; demand wording stays out.

article_slate.title: Sync Finish, two baskets, one dinner: what the setting promises and what to check.
article_slate.angle: Reads a named listing feature as a listing claim: what “Sync Finish” says it does, what the manual defines, and the three checks before relying on it for one shared dinner.
article_slate.provenance: SHOP-01’s listing title names Sync Finish; the feature description stays a listing claim, not a test result.

article_slate.title: What actually fits on the counter? Measure before you believe the quart number.
article_slate.angle: A measuring checklist: depth, width, ventilation clearance and door swing, with prompts to check the exact model’s manual — the numbers that matter are in the reader’s kitchen, not the listing.
article_slate.provenance: Extends the shipped cleanup-and-counter-space guide; dimensions stay unverified and the guide says so.

article_slate.title: Do presets change dinner, or just the label?
article_slate.angle: Follow-up to the multi-function guide: what a preset count claims, what a preset usually is, and why the manual matters more than the number on the box.
article_slate.provenance: SHOP-02’s listing title names 24 one-touch presets; the count is listing wording, not an endorsement.

article_slate.title: Wireless range claims: what “unlimited range” can and cannot promise.
article_slate.angle: Connectivity claims read carefully: what WiFi range wording describes, what the app requirements add, and the checks to run before hosting day.
article_slate.provenance: SHOP-05’s listing title names WiFi unlimited range; the claim stays a listing claim.

article_slate.title: Reading an air-fryer listing: five claims to separate from evidence.
article_slate.angle: The anti-slop flagship: teach the reader the method this site uses — listing claim, manual, independent evidence — so any shop page can be read with the same five questions.
article_slate.provenance: Google’s review-quality guidance (expertise, evidence, pros and cons from original research) and the FTC’s rule against talking about experience you do not have.

review_b9008684.prompt_intro: Lines this round would append to the design prompt if approved. Copying or appending them is an approval step for the reviewer; nothing is applied by reading this page.
review_b9008684.prompt_lines: Publish on a dated seasonal rhythm without ever claiming demand: a restrained seasonal strip names the calendar fact and links the guides that answer it. Grow the reading room one question-shaped guide at a time; each new guide keeps the same evidence limits, related-links mesh, Article schema, canonical URL, sitemap and RSS entry as the current six. Add FAQPage structured data only when every answer is already visible and sourced on the page. Keep the mobile-first type scale and 44-pixel tap targets, and make the format comparison reachable from long guides. Use labelled generic art until authorized exact-product assets exist, and label real imagery with its source and date when it arrives. Group the reading room by the decision a reader is facing. Every suggestion shows what evidence would change the decision; a review choice never implements itself. If paid search is ever used it lands on this site — never directly or indirectly on an Amazon Site — and organic findability starts with Search Console verification and a first-party query report.
